Good to slow down here — this is genuinely worth understanding before any code, because it's not really "one register," it's the point where several things we've been deliberately deferring all night come due at once.

**The concrete problem in GCD's structure**

Walk the actual wiring: `dualfanout`'s outputs feed `Mod` and loop back into `dualfanin`, whose output feeds `EQ0`/`LTsteer`, whose output steers `dualfanout` again. That's a real cycle — the *same* piece of combinational logic needs to process a value, feed its own output back as its own next input, and do this repeatedly until `EQ0` says stop. In synchronous logic you'd reach for a clocked register without thinking about it. NCL has no clock, so "hold this value until it's safe to advance" has to be expressed entirely through completeness — the same NULL/DATA alternation that's been doing all the work in every combinational gate we've emitted so far, just now needing to *persist* across iterations instead of resolving once and being done.

**Why this is more than "add a register" — it's where deferred semantics come due**

Look at what's actually sitting in this file that's been captured as *opaque text* all night, purely syntactically:

* The `{...}` mutex/conditional groups (`{$inlesser $remainder}{$ingreater $cyclelesser}`) — captured as a sentinel `Place`, never interpreted.
* The `[...]` bundle brackets — same treatment.
* `$steer( )` pure-value expressions selecting between `True[...]`/`False[...]` — captured as a `.pure_value` string, `export_vhdl.zig` currently just emits a `TODO` comment for it.
* The nested bundled conditional output in `dualfanout`'s invocation (`({(cyclelesser<> cyclegreater<>)(SINK<> GCD<>)})`) — this is literally the mechanism that decides "keep looping" vs. "done, emit the answer, discard the rest into `SINK`." Right now it's opaque text too.

**Every one of those needs real meaning for GCD to actually work** — not just the feedback loop. `$steer()` has to actually evaluate to `True`/`False` and route data accordingly; the conditional output group has to actually gate which destination receives the value. That's the real reason it's a different scale of task than items 1–8, not just a bigger version of the same kind of patch.

**The actual NCL mechanism, at a conceptual level (not code)**

The general pattern for holding state in NCL — sometimes called a wave-pipeline register — works roughly like this: a storage stage only accepts a new DATA value once its *previous* output has been consumed and acknowledged back to NULL by whatever's downstream; it only releases that NULL and re-arms once the new input is genuinely complete. So instead of "on clock edge, latch," it's "on completeness of input AND confirmation that output has returned to NULL, transition; on completeness of the *next* input, transition again." That's the general async-registration idea, and I'm reasonably confident in it as *general* NCL/asynchronous design theory.

**What I'm not confident about, and where I'd stop rather than guess:** whether *this specific* iterative-loop pattern — one wavefront cycling through the same logic repeatedly until a termination condition, as opposed to a pipeline advancing a stream of *different* wavefronts — is something Fant addresses explicitly, with his own specific terminology and circuit convention, somewhere later in the book. Chapter 12 (everything we've transcribed so far) is purely the Invocation Language's syntax; registration, pipelining, and iteration feel like they'd belong to a later chapter given the paper's own framing that "sequentiality is a degenerate case of concurrency." I'd rather check whether that chapter exists and transcribe it the same disciplined way we did chapter 12, than design a register primitive from general async-logic knowledge and risk it not matching Fant's actual model — same "book is ground truth" discipline that's kept the parser honest all night.
